Codenames vs Decrypto: Which Word Game Wins Game Night

2026-09-18

You narrowed it down to two games. Codenames and Decrypto. Both are word games. Both run on teams. Both show up on every "best party game" list you can find. But they feel completely different. I own both. I have played each more than 20 times. And I will tell you straight: there is no single winner. There is a right pick for your exact group.

This is a common dead end. You search "best party game for game night," and these two names keep coming up. You add both to your cart, then stare at them, not sure which one to actually get. I ran into the same wall. So I bought both over a couple of years, put them in front of different crowds, and tracked which one earned its shelf space. Here is what I learned.

The One-Line Version First

If you want a game that works from round one with a loud, mixed group: get Codenames. If you want a game that rewards the same small group playing together every week: get Decrypto. That is the honest answer. Now here is why, and why the answer is not as obvious as the ratings suggest.

Side by Side: The Specs That Matter

CodenamesDecrypto
Price$24.97$24.99
Players4-83-8
Playtime15 min30 min
Age14+12+
Complexity1.2 (easy)2.0 (medium)

Pay attention to the playtime and complexity rows. Those two numbers explain most of the difference between these games. Codenames is light and fast. Decrypto is heavier and slower. Neither is bad. They just serve different nights.

Codenames: The Game That Works With Anyone

Codenames splits your group into two teams. Each team has a spymaster who sees the secret key and gives one-word clues. Their teammates point at the words on the table, trying to hit their own cards and avoid the assassin. Get the assassin and you lose instantly. Rules take 60 seconds. A round takes 15 minutes.

My first game was at a house party with 8 people who had never played a modern board game. I was nervous explaining it. By the second round, one guest was leaning over the table, tapping cards, convincing her whole team. That is Codenames. It turns non-gamers into loud, competitive players within minutes. The best clue I ever heard: someone said "hydro" and four of her teammates all pointed at "water" at the same time. Everyone lost it.

However, there is a cost. When a spymaster gives a bad clue, that player is stuck watching the board for the rest of the round. Codenames is not eliminations like a deathmatch, but one bad guess can bench you mentally for 15 minutes. And it really needs at least 4 players to feel balanced. Two on two is fine. Solo spymaster games feel flat.

Here is the part I did not expect: Decrypto has a higher rating on BoardGameGeek (8.0 vs Codenames' 7.7). So I assumed it must simply be the better game. It is not that clean. The game I pull off the shelf more often is still Codenames. Because friction rules everything. Codenames explains itself in one round and finishes in 15 minutes. Decrypto needs a full example round before the table clicks, then runs 30. In the time it takes to explain Decrypto, you have played a whole game of Codenames and started a second one.

Decrypto: The Game That Gets Better Every Week

Decrypto is the deeper sibling. Two teams of two or three each hold four secret words. Every round, one player on the team gives three clues that secretly point to their words, in order. Your teammates have to figure out which clue matches which word. But the other team is watching. If they can decode your team's cipher before yours does, they steal the win. There is no quick elimination. Nobody sits out. Every player on both teams is engaged for the full 30 minutes.

The first time I played, I looked at the keywords and codes and thought, this feels like homework. I almost shelved it. Then I gave it one more night with three friends who play games every Thursday. That is where it woke up. By our third game, we were leaving subtle traps. I gave a clue that was almost too obvious for my own team, hoping to bait the other side into guessing my code. They fell for it and I won with a clean score. It was the most satisfying party game moment I have had in years.

Here is the key insight about Decrypto's tension. In Codenames, the enemy cannot touch your clue. In Decrypto, they can track it, decode it, and beat you with your own words. That pressure changes how you talk. You stop giving the obvious clue and start getting creative. The game respects players who think. It is why the rating is so high: people who own it play it dozens of times.

So Which One Should You Buy?

Here is how I decide, and it comes down to one question: does your group change every week, or is it the same people every week?

If your group changes every week, or has anyone who has never played a modern board game, get Codenames. It is the fastest path to a great first game night. Zero risk. It is $24.97 and plays in 15 minutes.

If you have a small group of 4-6 who play together regularly and want something with real depth, get Decrypto. It costs about the same ($24.99) but gives you a game that gets better the 5th and 10th time you play it. It is the smarter long-term buy for a committed group.

One more option worth naming. If your group gets competitive and someone handles losing badly, skip both and get a cooperative word game instead. Just One (about $24) has everyone helping one player guess a word, and it is impossible to single anyone out. It is the friendliest of the three. It is what I reach for when the night has guests who do not want to fight.

The Shelf Test: would these games survive 10 plays on your shelf? Codenames yes, but only if your group changes. Same four people will burn through it in a few months of weekly nights. Decrypto yes, and it gets better with repetition. Same group, 10 plays in, still tense. I have owned Codenames for 4 years. It still hits the table at least once a month. It has earned its spot. But on my own shelf, the game I actually look forward to now is Decrypto.

Both prices hover in the same $24-30 band and bounce around on Amazon. If you see either under $26, that is a solid deal; grab it. If you still cannot pick, start with Codenames, then add Decrypto a few months later once the group is hooked. That is exactly the order I did it, and I ended up with a full cabinet of party games.
